Two Farmers and a Cow: our Kaggriculture story (explained simply)

Team Chris Deotte. Final result: rank 439 of 10,246 teams. Built by one human and a team of five AI agents in the last ten days.

Kaggriculture is a farming game. You run a farm for 30 days against one other farmer. You plant crops, raise animals, hire helpers, and sell what you make at a market. The catch: you and your rival sell into the same market, so when they sell, your prices fall. Most money at the end wins.

We shipped two very different bots. Here is what they are, in plain words, and what we learned.

Part 1: The tape bot (v35), final rating 1960, rank 658

What is a tape bot?

Early in the competition a brilliant public notebook appeared, "The 2945 Farm". It plays the game like a music tape: the same script every game. Day 0 buy seeds, day 1 hire helpers, day 5 plant strawberries, day 11 plant a big strawberry block, from day 12 buy and sell wheat lots, day 29 sell everything. It never looks at what the rival is doing. And it was very good: it reached a 2945 rating when it was published.

What we added

We did not submit the notebook as it was (that is never a good idea). We rebuilt it in our own code, checked that it played the exact same game to the dollar, and then glued three layers on top:

  1. Sale layer: sell each product in the hours when the market pays the most.
  2. Hold 8: from day 20, keep 8 items back instead of dumping everything, so prices stay higher for the rest.
  3. Phase selector: in the late game, pick the wheat-lot size (60) that won most often in our local tests.

Every layer was tested the same way: play the new bot and the old bot on the same 400 random worlds and count who makes more money. Each layer was worth a few hundred dollars a game. Over three weeks the tape went from our v16 to v35.

Why the tape bot stalled

Hundreds of teams copied the same public notebook. When a tape plays a tape, it is a coin flip: after the deadline our v35 won exactly 50 percent of its games against other tapes, with a median margin of 29 dollars. And above a rating of 2100 the opponents were not tapes anymore. They were farmers with animals.

Part 2: The cow bot (W3n + wash), final rating 2125, rank 439

The idea: copy the farmers who win

Four days before the deadline we looked at the replays of the top teams and noticed something: almost all of them start with one cow on turn one and build a real farm economy around it, instead of the tape's crops-only plan. Cows give milk and sheep give wool every day for the whole game; a crop pays only when you harvest it. So we did what Chris said: "copy them and improve it."

How the cow bot starts

On the very first turn it spends everything: two cows, three sheep, four hired hands, six melon seeds, ten wheat seeds and a little wheat to feed the animals. One shopping list, and every hand and seed is at work from hour 1.

How the farm is laid out

The farm has four quadrants, but the fourth one costs money and hands you never get back. The cow bot buys three and never the fourth: wheat and melons near the shed, pastures for the herd, and strawberries from day 2.

How we built it: one measured change at a time

We started by copying the winners' opening exactly. That first version won only 17 percent of its games against our own tape. Then, every hour, a different agent tried one change, and we kept only the changes that won more games on the same 400 worlds. In 40 hours the win rate went from 17 percent to 67 percent.

The changes that mattered, in order:

  • Three quadrants and a day-6 herd wave: on day 6 buy a second wave of animals, sized by which shops have opened in town (sheep if there is a yarn store, geese only if there is an egg shop, cows for milk shops).
  • Late-game knobs: when melons are harvested, how far animals may be from the shed, when buying stops (day 14).
  • A day-10 melon rush, with the melons planted right beside the shed so they are quick to carry.
  • Route targets and fertiliser reservation: from day 12 a scheduler plans each helper's walking route for the day and keeps fertiliser back for the jobs that need it.
  • Route repair and route swapping: if a plan breaks mid-day (a helper got blocked, a sale failed), fix it instead of idling, and let two helpers swap the tails of their routes when that is shorter.
  • The one-list day 0 shown above (worth about 7 percentage points on its own).

The last trick: the wheat wash

Many rival tapes are "floaters": every few hours they buy a big wheat lot to resell later. Market orders settle one slot at a time, so we added a tiny trick. When we detect a floater, we buy 60 wheat first in the turn and sell the same 60 back last in the same turn. We end up where we started; the rival pays a higher price for its lot. It fires in about one game in ten and is worth about 1,000 dollars when it does.

Part 3: What happened on the leaderboard

The cow bot finished at 2125, rank 439, and the tape bot at 1960, rank 658. Both bots played every hosted game exactly as they played locally (we checked every single game step by step), so the ranks are what the bots are worth.

What we learned

After the deadline we downloaded all 352 of our games and sorted the opponents into families. Tape bots split their games with us. Economy bots, the ones with real herds, beat both of our bots by 5,000 to 8,000 dollars a game. The top teams' write-ups later confirmed why: they trained neural networks that imitate the best farmers from thousands of replays, and those networks run a better farm than any schedule we could write by hand.

So the honest moral of the story: copy the economy, not the schedule, and start on day one. Thanks to the organizers for a wonderful game, and to every team whose replays taught our cow bot how to farm.

Methods, for the curious: a bit-exact local re-simulation of the game engine, paired-seed evaluation (same worlds for both bots), an hourly identity check of every hosted game against the local twin, and an official-runner check of every archive before upload. The whole competition was run by five AI agents (Fable as lead, Astra, two Opus builders and a second Fable on evaluation) with Chris directing.

Great writeup and I love your wheat wash trick it's quite clever. Also, your conclusions match mine closely. Tape-vs-tape is a coin flip, and imitating top replays with a network was what moved me from around 87% to around 102% of the top player's coins in their own seats. Two things that might interest you is that I found gains measured against my own previous bot often didn't transfer while replaying recorded top players' games exactly (their moves pinned but the market live) was a far better gate. For the part about the 4th quadrant unlock in my close ladder losses, the winners averaged 3.46 quadrants to my 3.00 and used the extra one for late tomatoes and wool. They sold twice my tomatoes, around 5k coins each game, which was more than enough to flip those games. It doesn't pay in every game, but the top players commit to it early in the ones where it does. After seeing that I tried to work on the 4th quadrant but forcing it hurt performance a lot. In the end I didn't have enough time to experiment more on that and unfortunately couldn't get my latest submission through in time, but it's alright since the experience is what mattered. Congrats on the silver 🎉

Thanks. When you trained your NN bot, did you train on multiple high scoring teams replay (at the same time, in one training)? Or did you train multiple NN bots with each on one team? This is something I've read in other writeups. Certain teams were easier to copy than other teams.

while replaying recorded top players' games exactly (their moves pinned but the market live) was a far better gate

I did this trick too. My agents called it "ghost bots" and they played new versions of their submissions on ghost bots.
